Biomolecules 3D Lab

Setting up the lab…

Biomolecules 3D Lab

A nutrition label says how much carbohydrate, protein and fat is in your food. But how does anyone find out? Run the four classic food tests on a 3D lab bench and use them to identify three mystery samples. Then build the molecules themselves, atom by atom, to see what a carbohydrate, a protein, a fat and DNA really are. Works offline in any modern browser — no internet, login or install.

🧪 Four tests

iodine → starch · Benedict’s → sugar · biuret → protein · paper → lipid

Each reagent changes color only when one kind of molecule is there. Always run controls so you know what “yes” and “no” look like.

🧱 The big idea

small units − water → big molecules

Cells join small units by removing water (dehydration synthesis) and split them by adding it back (hydrolysis). The atoms in your food become the atoms in you.

3D lab furniture, equipment and foods (cabinets, lab bottles, clock, stools, safety glasses, sink, first-aid cabinet, extinguisher, SDS binder, steel table, potato, apple, milk carton, chip bag, cheese, tuna can, sugar box, egg): NVIDIA SimReady assets, licensed under CC BY 4.0; converted from OpenUSD and simplified for offline use. Teacher notes

Two self-contained labs in one offline HTML file for grades 9–12 biology. Open it in Chrome, Edge, Safari or Firefox (Chromebooks and iPads included). Nothing is uploaded; results are saved in the browser on that device only, and students can download their data as a CSV file.

Learning goals

Students will be able to:

  • Carry out the iodine, Benedict’s, biuret and brown paper tests and interpret the results.
  • Explain why positive and negative controls are needed.
  • Identify unknown foods from a pattern of test results, using claim, evidence and reasoning.
  • Name the building blocks of carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids, and the elements in each.
  • Model dehydration synthesis and hydrolysis, and count the atoms and water molecules involved.

Suggested sequence (2 class periods)

  • Lab 1 · Food Tests (1 period): The four food tests on five controls and seven foods, recording the color each time; then three mystery samples (chosen at random from the seven foods for each student) identified by matching their results.
  • Lab 2 · Build the Molecules (1 period): Ball-and-stick models of glucose, amino acids, a triglyceride and nucleotides; dehydration synthesis and hydrolysis; counting atoms and water molecules; which elements each class contains.

What the models assume

  • Lab 1 results are idealized so each food has a clear, unique pattern. Real foods are messier: milk gives a moderate Benedict’s result (lactose), potato may give a trace of sugar, and cheese can vary. Table sugar (sucrose) is a non-reducing sugar, so it stays blue.
  • The Benedict’s test is shown as semi-quantitative: blue (none), green (trace), yellow, orange, brick red (a lot).
  • The lipid test is the brown paper (grease spot) test, chosen because it needs no hazardous stain. Sudan III or IV and the ethanol emulsion test are alternatives in the hands-on version.
  • Lab 2 molecules have the correct atoms and bonds, but bond angles and shapes are tidied up. Fatty acids are shortened to 6 carbons. Nucleotides are drawn as a schematic without hydrogen atoms.

Misconceptions these labs target

  • “Benedict’s solution detects all sugars.” Table sugar tastes sweet but stays blue; students compare it with glucose.
  • “A food contains only one kind of biomolecule.” Milk, cheese and potato chips test positive for two or three.
  • “Fats are long chains of repeating units, like starch.” Lab 2 builds a fat from one glycerol and exactly three fatty acids.
  • “Fats and oils are different kinds of molecule.” Switching to unsaturated fatty acids changes only the double bonds.
  • “Atoms are lost when molecules join.” Students count atoms before and after: the “missing” H and O leave as water.

Standards

  • NGSS: HS-LS1-6 (Construct and revise an explanation for how carbon, hydrogen and oxygen from sugar molecules may combine with other elements to form amino acids and other large carbon-based molecules.). Supports HS-LS1-1. Practices: Planning and Carrying Out Investigations; Analyzing and Interpreting Data; Developing and Using Models; Engaging in Argument from Evidence. Crosscutting concepts: Energy and Matter; Structure and Function; Patterns.
  • Texas TEKS (Biology, §112.42, adopted 2021): B.5A (relate the functions of carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids to the structure and function of a cell). Scientific and engineering practices: B.1B, B.1C, B.1E, B.1F, B.1G, B.3A.
  • Common Core: RST.9-10.3 (follow precisely a multistep procedure when carrying out experiments and taking measurements); RST.9-10.7 (translate information between words, tables, graphs and equations); WHST.9-10.1 (write arguments focused on discipline-specific content (claim, evidence, reasoning)).
  • AP Biology (2025 course framework): 1.3 Introduction to Macromolecules; 1.4 Carbohydrates; 1.5 Lipids; 1.6 Nucleic Acids; 1.7 Proteins.

Safety and risk assessment

Using the simulation (screen only: no chemicals or equipment)

HazardWhat could happenHow to control it
Screen useEye strain, poor postureEach lab fits one class period. Build in a short break; look away from the screen every 20 minutes.
Flashing or moving imagesPhotosensitivity, motion discomfortNo flashing or strobing content. The 3D camera moves only when the student moves it; fly-through moves become instant jumps when the device is set to reduce motion.
Student dataPrivacyRuns offline. No accounts, no tracking and nothing uploaded. Results stay in the browser on that device and can be cleared at any time.

Food tests (optional hands-on version of Lab 1)

HazardWhat could happenHow to control it
Benedict’s solution (contains copper(II) sulfate)Harmful if swallowed; irritates eyes and skin; toxic to aquatic lifeSplash goggles and gloves; rinse splashes at once. Collect waste as your district requires; do not pour copper solutions down the sink unless permitted.
Biuret reagent (sodium hydroxide and copper(II) sulfate)Corrosive to eyes and skinSplash goggles and gloves; small dropper bottles; rinse splashes with plenty of water.
Iodine–potassium iodide solutionStains skin and clothes; irritates eyes; harmful if swallowedSplash goggles and gloves; small dropper bottles.
Hot water bath for Benedict’s testScalds; hot liquid can spurt from a tubeUse a hot water bath, not a flame. Use a test tube holder and point tubes away from faces.
Glass test tubesCuts from broken glassUse a rack; put broken glass in a broken-glass container with a brush and dustpan.
Food samplesAllergic reactions; eating contaminated foodCheck for allergies (milk, egg, fish, and peanut or tree nuts if you add them) before handing out samples. No tasting, eating or drinking.

This table supports, but does not replace, your own school or district risk assessment. Follow your chemical hygiene plan, read the SDS for every chemical, and check state and district rules before any hands-on activity.

Accessibility

  • Every color result is also named in words on its button and in the results table, so the lab does not depend on color vision.
  • Positive and negative results are marked + and −.
  • All controls work with the keyboard: Tab to move, Enter or Space to press, arrow keys on sliders. In the 3D view, arrow keys rotate and the + and − keys zoom.
  • Gray controls cannot be used yet. They stay reachable and explain why when pressed.
  • Nothing is shown by color alone: right and wrong answers are marked ✓ and ✗, and results are given in words and numbers.
  • No sound, no flashing content, and no time limits that cannot be repeated. Text stays readable when the browser is zoomed to 200%.

Controls

  • Drag to rotate · scroll or pinch to zoom · right-drag or two-finger drag to pan.
